items.titleEn: Gold climbs above $4,000, Wall Street rallies as Dems take Congress - Kitco PM Report
items.summaryEn: (Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply higher in late U.S. trading Wednesday, as Democrats' sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections sent the dollar, Treasury yields and crude oil prices lower, encouraging renewed buying interest in precious metals. The election results handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, raising expectations for legislative gridlock and potentially more restrained fiscal spending during the remainder of President Donald Trump's term. Hopes for renewed negotiations between Washington and Tehran also helped reduce the geopolitical risk premium in energy markets, providing additional relief from inflation concerns. At the latest verified afternoon quotation, spot gold was trading near $4,065.90 an ounce, up $136.50, or 3.47%, while spot silver was trading near $52.280, up $2.608, or 5.25%, on the session. Both metals recovered strongly from October's steep losses, with silver outperforming gold as lower borrowing costs and a weaker dollar supported precious metals. Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections produced a decisive shift in the balance of power in Washington, with Democrats winning control of both the House of Representatives and Senate. The victories ended Republican control of Congress and raised expectations that the administration will face substantial obstacles in advancing additional tax reductions, fiscal spending initiatives and legislation affecting energy, technology and financial markets. Investors interpreted the outcome as potentially restraining future fiscal expansion and federal borrowing requirements, although substantial budget deficits and existing spending commitments remain important constraints. The results also increase the likelihood of congressional scrutiny of artificial intelligence investment, federal energy policy and U.S. military operations involving Iran. However, the extent of any policy changes will depend on negotiations between Congress and the White House, and the election outcome does not directly alter Federal Reserve monetary policy.
